items.title: Terry Gibbs interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 12, 2001 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: We’ve been playing together as co-leaders and we have never come close to having an argument.

ctx.x: Well just concerts and festivals and college things. That’s all I want to do. My best job actually is a college thing because first of all Yamaha sponsors me, you know, the college can only afford to pay me two dollars, they pay the rest. I made a deal with Yamaha to use their instrument. They supply me with instruments everywhere I go. I put a price on my clinic, like I said, on my job. And I use the Dream Band music more than anything. I send out about eight charts, everybody wants to play it. And the band…

Saturday afternoon and do a clinic even though they know the charts, just a little edges I want. I don’t try to step on the band leader and make him look like he doesn’t know what he’s doing. Because he’s already there, and I’d have to spend like another week to get it like I wanted. But it’s so good, the music is so good, sixty percent of it is so good that sixty percent will sound good, no matter if they make mistakes. It’s there. And I do a clinic and I play the concert at night and go home the next day. I…
Good one. All right. Well listen, I hope you have a safe trip home. Best of luck with your upcoming things, and I really appreciate your time.

items.title: Terry Gibbs interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 5, 2021 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: Well Buddy DeFranco and I recorded it at a slower tempo

ctx.x: Yes. Well he did — not me. He did show up on my job, this is when I was just learning bebop of which unfortunately he showed up and scared the hell out of me. If you notice where I write in my book that first of all you’d walk down to Birdland and he’d be standing there and he’d say, “Give me a quarter” or “give me a half dollar.” That was a lot of money in those days. And, and these musicians would say, “I don’t have it.” And he’d say, “Where are you playing tomorrow I’ll come and sit in with you.” And they gave…

it was only a 32 bar chorus. On the 30th bar, because I knew I wanted to see him go into another chorus, I bent down to tie my shoe. I was on the floor. When he started to play more I got up so then when the 30 bars came closer to 30 bars I went down and tied my shoe. And then once again I had loosened my vibes, I had tied them down — I didn’t know what I was doing. But after about 16 choruses on the floor, my piano player who didn’t think he was even going to follow him because I would come in next, got panicked…
At that point, about that time with the Charlie Parker incident were you in your early twenties?

items.title: DeFranco Buddy — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: No, Terry, there was no conflict, Terry was the leader.

ctx.x: And was there ever any conflict between who was leading? I mean you were really co-leaders, weren’t you?
No, Terry, there was no conflict, Terry was the leader. [laughter] I know, I mean, it’s…
